I understand that bitcoin is used by a lot of people even today, but I feel that it's not exactly ready for mainstream adoption.

It's too easy to steal bitcoin from average users.

There's no security at all if you lose your private key or it gets stolen. It's gone.

It's too hard to get bitcoin.

Not many mainstream sites accept bitcoin.

So what needs to happen for bitcoin to be usable by a woman in her 50s? I would argue that bitcoin has to be easy to use and secure for the least intelligent and technical people for it to be adopted by the mainstream.
How can bitcoin become a useful mainstream currency?

There's no security at all if you lose your private key or it gets stolen. It's gone.

Bitcoin's are like cash. If you lose cash, it's gone. No way around it... well there is, is it's called a bank. Banks provide that extra security that cold hard cash does not. If there 's a place in the market for bitcoin bank like services (think coinbase, maybe better) then it will be filled, but it will probably come with some of the same drawbacks as banks do (not actually having direct access to your funds).

It's too easy to steal bitcoin from average users.

The problem is that it's way to easy to steal anything from your average users' computers. Your private keys aren't safe if the password you use to encrypt them is 12345 and you click next, next, next, finish or ok/yes to every single dialog box that pops up. The personal computer culture is a security travesty and personally I don't think it'll ever get better. The only place where it is better is in the mobile space, where the device is far less in the control of the users (non jailbroke iphones and non rooted android devices).

It's sounds counter intuitive but bitcoins on your average user's iphone is much safer than anywhere else (unless your considering paper wallets/cold storage).

But at the end of the day the solution is the same as before, something like a bank.

It's too hard to get bitcoin.

It's only hard if your trying to keep your trade private ( I assume your hypothetical 50 your old woman doesn't care about privacy and has access to traditional banking services). KYC and anti money laundering regulations make keeping your trades private near impossible, unless you're willing to use localbitcoin, but then yes, it's hard.

I personally buy mine at two exchanges that have copies of my photo IDs. Never had any problem nor ever felt like it was hard.

Not many mainstream sites accept bitcoin.

Bitcoin isn't going to find its niche in mainstream sites, not now at least. Other than Overstock and Microsoft I don't know of any site that does and even if they did most people would still use credit cards. The main use of bitcoin right now is in places where traditional financial services are too expensive (remittance) and where friction is too high (regional and capital controls). I've bought some ebooks that were unavailable in my region before, it was pretty easy and felt like a total rebel (I know, dork right?!).

The only value proposition to your average consumer that I find convincing actually is in security. After several Bitcoin purchases, buying online by throwing around personal information and credit card numbers just seems like disaster waiting to happen.

For bitcoin to be easy and safe to use for the least intelligent and technical people it needs to be managed by a company and act pretty much like, paypal, venmo, google wallet, facebook payments, etc..

I think coinbase, changetip, and circle make it pretty easy to spend and accept bitcoin, but those bitcoins aren't strictly under your control. If the company service goes down you cannot spend your money even if the bitcoin network is unaffected.

Dead-simple transactions. Think how easy it is to changetip someone, when you have a changetip account set up (but without a centralized account).

She should be able to go to an Amazon page, and click "Pay with Bitcoin". She'll get a secure dialog asking to confirm it (so another program can't fake-click the button). If her wallet is password-protected, she enters her password here. She clicks "Yes". Now she's paid Amazon.

This can't be malware-proof, and 50-year-old women are good at getting malware. You don't often hear about people losing their credit card info to malware - I don't know whether malware isn't common (which would be good) or because chargebacks exist (which would be bad for bitcoin as it doesn't have chargebacks).

PayPal and Google Wallet offer the same thing. It's hard to do this with fiat currencies, and impossible to do without allowing another group to influence your policies, because it relies on a large degree of "social integration".

For security, hard wallets seem to be the solution short term. Trezor and ledger wallets are lightweight and simple to use. While no one likes the idea of carrying around another electronic device besides their phone, it circumvents the need to have a centralized institution hold your money.
